headline: Reauthorizes and updates the federal missing children's assistance program, adding new uses for grant money and tighter grant rules through fiscal year 2018.
what_it_does: This law renews the Missing Children's Assistance Act and sets funding for fiscal years 2014 through 2018, including yearly grants to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. It adds new allowed uses for those grants, such as training law enforcement and schools to find missing children and helping with child sex trafficking cases. It also caps the pay of Center employees paid with federal funds at 110% of the Senior Executive Service maximum, and it adds audit, conference spending, and lobbying rules for grant recipients.

who_it_affects.group: Children who go missing, including foster children
who_it_affects.how: The law lets law enforcement work with child welfare agencies and schools to respond when children in the foster system or in school go missing.

who_it_affects.group: State and local law enforcement agencies
who_it_affects.how: They can receive federally funded technical help and training on finding and recovering missing children and children at risk of sex trafficking.

who_it_affects.group: Schools, teachers, and homeless shelter staff
who_it_affects.how: They may receive federally funded training on preventing child abduction and sexual exploitation and on helping locate missing children.

who_it_affects.group: National Center for Missing and Exploited Children
who_it_affects.how: It receives authorized annual grant funding with a cap on federally paid employee compensation and new rules on how grant money can be spent.

who_it_affects.group: Organizations that receive Justice Department grants
who_it_affects.how: They face Inspector General audits, possible two-year grant bans for unresolved unallowable costs, and a ban on using grant funds to lobby over grant awards.

when_it_takes_effect: The law was enacted on September 30, 2013, and its authorizations cover fiscal years 2014 through 2018.
